1081.quote_or_event: “Wonderful is the sound current of the Naad, wonderful is the knowledge of the Vedas.”
1081.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak begins a long salok of vismad (wonder), listing one thing after another in creation that leaves him astonished.
1081.tie_back: The Kural's hero is so bewildered by beauty that he cannot tell whether he sees a goddess, a peacock or a girl; Guru Nanak's vismad is the Sikh name for being overwhelmed and wonder-struck before the beauty of creation.
1081.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1081._accuracy_note: Next-best match: it shares the overwhelmed wonder, but the wonder is spiritual awe at God's creation, not romantic love.

1082.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, the True Guru, the Spiritual Warrior, has shot me with His Arrow. As soon as it struck me, I fell to the ground, with a hole in my heart.”
1082.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir describes the Guru's word as an arrow that strikes the devotee to the ground and pierces his heart.
1082.tie_back: The Kural says the woman's answering glance strikes like a goddess leading an army; Kabir uses the same image of being struck down by a warrior's single shot, here the Guru's word.
1082.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 194) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1082._accuracy_note: Good fit on the image of being struck down by a single attack, but Kabir speaks of spiritual, not romantic, love.

1083.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, the world is afraid of death - that death fills my mind with bliss.”
1083.explanation: In another salok, Kabir says the dying that the world fears, which Sikh commentators read as dying to the ego, fills him with joy.
1083.tie_back: The Kural's lover says he has only now met Death, in the form of a woman's large eyes; Kabir also speaks of meeting a death that love makes welcome.
1083.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1365, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1083._accuracy_note: Next-best match: both pair love with a kind of death, but Kabir means the death of ego in spiritual love, not romantic love, and lacks the Kural's playful hyperbole.

1084.quote_or_event: “The Bani of the Lord's Love is the pointed arrow, which has pierced my mind, O Lord King.”
1084.explanation: In a chhant in Raag Asa, Guru Ram Das describes the Guru's word of divine love as a sharp-pointed arrow that has wounded his mind.
1084.tie_back: The Kural marvels that a gentle, innocent girl has eyes that seem to drink the life of anyone who sees them; Guru Ram Das likewise finds that something sweet, the word of love, wounds like a sharp arrow.
1084.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 449, Raag Asa, Chhant, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1084._accuracy_note: Good fit on gentleness that wounds, but the love is spiritual, not romantic, and the wound comes from the Guru's word rather than a glance.

1085.quote_or_event: “You have thousands of eyes, and yet You have no eyes. You have thousands of forms, and yet You do not have even one.”
1085.explanation: In the evening prayer Sohila, Guru Nanak marvels at a God who has countless eyes and forms yet is beyond all form.
1085.tie_back: The Kural's lover cannot decide whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a shy doe, since it seems to hold all three natures; Guru Nanak is likewise baffled by a Beloved whose eyes and forms are many and none.
1085.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 13, Sohila, Raag Dhanasari, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1085._accuracy_note: Next-best match on bafflement at a look or form that holds several natures at once; this is spiritual wonder at the formless God, not romantic love.

1086.quote_or_event: “The soul-bride and the Husband Lord live together as one, but the hard wall of egotism has come between them.”
1086.explanation: Using the bride-soul image, Guru Ram Das says the soul and God already live together, but ego stands between them like a hard wall.
1086.tie_back: The Kural's lover wishes the curved brows would screen the girl's eyes; Gurbani also speaks of a screen between lover and Beloved, but there the screen is ego, and the devotee longs for it to be removed.
1086.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1263, Raag Malar, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1086._accuracy_note: Next-best match on the idea of a screen between lovers; the love is spiritual, not romantic, and Gurbani wants the barrier removed while the Kural's lover wants a protective screen.

1087.quote_or_event: “The mind is the elephant, the Guru is the elephant-driver, and knowledge is the whip. Wherever the Guru drives the mind, it goes.”
1087.explanation: In a salok of Gujri ki Vaar, Guru Amar Das compares the unruly mind to an elephant that obeys only when the Guru, as its driver, controls it with knowledge.
1087.tie_back: The Kural compares the cloth on a maiden's bosom to the face-cloth that restrains a raging elephant; Guru Amar Das also uses the restrained elephant, here the mind held in check by the Guru.
1087.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 516, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar (salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1087._accuracy_note: Next-best match built on a shared image of keeping a dangerous elephant in check; the Sikh verse is about spiritual discipline of the mind, not romantic love.

1088.quote_or_event: “Give up your selfhood, and so obtain your Husband Lord; what other clever tricks are of any use?”
1088.explanation: In Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak tells the soul-bride that only giving up her ego wins the Husband Lord, and that no cleverness can take its place.
1088.tie_back: The Kural's warrior, whose strength made enemies tremble, finds his might broken before one girl's bright forehead; Guru Nanak also teaches that pride and strength must give way in love.
1088.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 722, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1088._accuracy_note: Partial fit: both have pride yielding to love, but Gurbani speaks of spiritual, not romantic, love and calls for giving up ego willingly, while the Kural's warrior is overcome.

1089.quote_or_event: “Humility is the word, forgiveness is the virtue, and sweet speech is the magic mantra. Wear these three robes, O sister, and you will captivate your Husband Lord.”
1089.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the soul-bride that humility, forgiveness and sweet speech are the only dress she needs to win her Lord.
1089.tie_back: The Kural asks what use other ornaments are to a girl who already has a doe-like look and natural modesty; Farid likewise says inner virtues, not outward finery, are the bride's true adornment.
1089.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 127) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1089._accuracy_note: Strong fit on modesty and virtue as a bride's real ornament; the bride and Husband here are the soul and God, so the love is spiritual, not romantic.

1090.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the mind is intoxicated with the Naam, drinking in its Nectar. It remains absorbed in the Lord's Love.”
1090.explanation: Speaking to yogis who used intoxicants, Guru Nanak says the true intoxication is the mind drinking in the Naam (divine Name) and staying absorbed in God's love.
1090.tie_back: The Kural says strong drink delights only those who drink it, while love delights even those who merely look; Guru Nanak also sets love above wine, calling love of the Name the truer intoxication.
1090.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 360, Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1090._accuracy_note: Strong fit on love as an intoxication greater than drink, but the love is spiritual, not romantic, and the verse does not make the Kural's point about delight by sight alone.
